content.title: What is a Linked List?
content.description: A Linked List is a linear data structure where elements are stored in separate nodes connected through links (pointers).

content.content: Unlike arrays, Linked Lists do not store elements in contiguous memory locations. Instead, each element is stored inside a node that contains the actual data and a reference to the next node.

content.title: Key Difference
content.content: Arrays rely on contiguous memory, while Linked Lists use references to connect nodes dynamically.
Why Do We Need Linked Lists?
Arrays have fixed sizes and expensive insertion/deletion operations. Linked Lists solve these problems by allowing dynamic memory allocation and efficient modifications.
Structure of a Node
The basic building block of a Linked List is a node. Every node contains two parts: data and a pointer (reference) to the next node.

content.title: Node Components
content.description: Data stores the actual value, while Next stores the memory address of the following node.

content.content: Linked List Representation

content.title: Head Pointer
content.content: The Head pointer stores the address of the first node in the Linked List.
How Linking Works
Each node stores the address of the next node. By following these links, we can traverse the entire Linked List.

content.title: Address Connections
steps: Node A → Address of Node B
Node B → Address of Node C
Node C → Address of Node D

content.content: Memory Allocation
Linked Lists allocate memory dynamically at runtime. Nodes can be created whenever needed without requiring contiguous memory blocks.

content.title: Dynamic Nature
content.content: Nodes can exist anywhere in memory because references connect them logically.
Types of Linked Lists

items.question: Singly Linked List
items.answer: Each node points to the next node only.

items.question: Doubly Linked List
items.answer: Each node stores previous and next references.

items.question: Circular Linked List
items.answer: Last node points back to the first node.

items.question: Circular Doubly Linked List
items.answer: Both previous and next references form a circle.

content.content: Traversal in Linked List
Traversal means visiting nodes one by one, starting from the head and following the next references until NULL is reached.
Advantages of Linked Lists

items.question: Dynamic Size
items.answer: Can grow and shrink during execution.

content.content: Disadvantages of Linked Lists

items.question: No Random Access
items.answer: Cannot directly access an element by index.

content.title: Common Mistake
content.content: Many beginners confuse node values with node addresses. Remember: pointers store addresses, not data values.

content.title: Interview Insight
content.description: Linked Lists are one of the most frequently asked interview topics because they test understanding of pointers, memory allocation, and data structure manipulation.
